historical_transitions.summary: A real PairCreated transaction anchors this runtime checkpoint; pair creation is not labeled a governance mutation. Both archive RPCs match the original factory runtime. feeToSetter is the Operations Safe 0x19B3Eb3Af5D93b77a5619b047De0EED7115A19e7, observed at threshold 3 with 6 owners; migrator is zero and feeTo is 0x5ad6211cd3fde39a9cecb5df6f380b8263d1e277. One enabled Safe module is observed at this snapshot; its separate authorization policy is outside this owner-threshold comparison.

At 15:13:11 UTC, a successful batch executes through the Operations Safe and contains factory setFeeTo(address) calldata. Both RPCs show feeTo=0x5ad6211cd3fde39a9cecb5df6f380b8263d1e277 at 23940492 and feeTo=0x1d2af2b99e253b68d72c76484dd88ffb0ace158c at 23940493. Receipt includes Safe ExecutionSuccess logs; threshold 3 and 6 owners remain. This is fee-routing configuration, not an implementation upgrade.

Operations Safe emits RemovedOwner at 21:51:23 UTC. Both RPCs verify getOwners() shrinks from 6 to 5 across 24300285/24300286 while getThreshold() stays 3. The Safe remains the factory feeToSetter; removing one signer changes the governing population, not the factory runtime or the three-signature execution threshold.

A real PairCreated transaction anchors the end checkpoint at 11:49:47 UTC. Both RPCs recover unchanged factory bytecode and the same Operations Safe as feeToSetter, with threshold 3 and 5 owners. feeTo remains 0x1d2af2b99e253b68d72c76484dd88ffb0ace158c and migrator remains zero. These are dated observations, not an assertion that administrative settings were immutable between snapshots. getModulesPaginated returns an empty module list at this endpoint.

evidence_sources.claim_summary: Archived first-party whitepaper identifies the Operations Safe at 0x19B3Eb3Af5D93b77a5619b047De0EED7115A19e7 and states that core-team actions must pass it with at least 3 signatures. It includes a transition warning about address lists. The checked commitment is the minimum signature count, not a promise that its six-member roster never changes.

Official repository initial commit includes deployments/ethereum/UniswapV2Factory.json binding the primary address and contracts/UniswapV2Factory.sol. The factory implementation section exactly matches the verified flattened deployment source. setFeeTo, setMigrator and setFeeToSetter all require msg.sender==feeToSetter.

Second independently dated whitepaper capture retains the at-least-3-signature Operations Safe commitment and the historical six-member roster. The roster is used as historical context, not asserted to be a current membership guarantee. Both archived PDFs were retrieved successfully; the original live PDF URL now returns 404.

Default-branch head retains the same Ethereum factory deployment address and implementation. This provides a later public source anchor. The separate mutable Safe roster and factory fee recipient must be re-read on chain; stable factory runtime does not freeze those administrative controls.

gap_windows.summary: Across the 1246-calendar-day observation span, published factory role gating and the archived numeric owner-signature threshold align with the sampled values. No repair time is measured, so mttr_days=null. zero_gap_verified is limited to that stored threshold and factory source model. One enabled module in 2023 and none at the 2026 endpoint were observed; earlier module authorization was not assessed, so no universal minimum-signature guarantee or exhaustive documentation alignment is certified.

executive_risk_memo:
SushiSwap's Ethereum V2 factory has stable deployed bytecode but retains mutable administrative authority through feeToSetter. The two archive providers recover the same verified runtime at the original 2020 deployment and the June 2023 and November 2026 checkpoints. The official source and deployment manifest bind this exact factory and gate fee recipient, migrator and authority reassignment behind feeToSetter. That address is the Operations Safe. Archived first-party whitepapers specify at least three signatures, and all sampled stored Safe owner thresholds equal three. The fee recipient changed in a successful December 2025 batch, independently bounded by before/after block reads and supported by matching setter calldata and Safe success logs. A January 2026 RemovedOwner event reduces the Safe from six owners to five while preserving the threshold. The stored owner-execution threshold remains three; owner-path liveness redundancy falls by one signer. Both RPCs also return one enabled module (0xCFbFaC74C26F8647cBDb8c5caf80BB5b32E43134) at the 2023 snapshot and none at the 2026 endpoint. Its historical authorization policy was not assessed, so this dossier does not certify that every execution path required three owner signatures. No inference about signer independence is made.

Forensics therefore records zero_gap_verified narrowly for the sampled factory permission model and numeric stored owner-signature threshold over a 1,246-calendar-day observation span. This is not a blanket finding that all Sushi documentation is current or that every intermediate configuration was checked. The archived paper's address-transition caveat is preserved, and its historical roster is not treated as a current guarantee. Its original live PDF URL is unavailable on review; no precise removal date or documentary repair interval was established. MTTR is null because no repair of a proven scoped contradiction is measured, rather than being reported as an invented zero-day fix.

The engineering census covers only sushiswap/v2-core default-branch ancestry at a349882c918c752d0363e4c6e02dedcbc48b734e from 2025-11-20T00:00:00Z through 2026-11-20T00:00:00Z. There are zero commits, contract or otherwise, and no active non-bot contributors in that window; bus_factor=0 denotes repository dormancy, not zero operational risk or inactivity across all Sushi repositories. code_before_upgrade_verified=false conservatively avoids claiming a code-first publication audit of the original 2020 deployment or every Sushi release. The observed changes are configuration and signer changes, not factory implementation upgrades. Consumers should distinguish immutable bytecode from an Operations Safe's continuing ability to redirect fees, assign a migrator, or replace its own governing authority, and should refresh current signer and parameter disclosures separately.
